subsystems.name: application
subsystems.capability: The application itself: routes, routers, app state, lifespan, and errors rendered as RFC 9457 problem details
subsystems.policy: Configuration is how Wreath starts; state is what it holds while running. They do not share an API. Route tables compile at startup, never per request. Dispatch is chosen at compile time too: `_select_dispatch` picks `_handle_http_plain` for an application with no global hooks and no dynamic matcher, and every delegation from it back to `_handle_http` must be decided *before* the specialized path has any effect a second dispatch would repeat -- before the Request exists, before a hook could run, before the recorder is told anything. A route handler may be `def` as well as `async def`; dispatch calls it and awaits only what came back awaitable, and every wrapper (binder, response validator, status coercion) preserves whichever convention it was handed. `_reject_session_after_authentication` scans **every** route-scoped registration -- `add_middleware`, `Router(middleware=[...])`, an included router's, and one route's `middleware=[...]` -- not just the application's. It used to read `self._middleware` alone, so a session middleware on a router walked past a refusal that had nothing to look at and shipped the 401 it exists to prevent (docs/decisions/0024). Nesting needs no special case: `Router.routes` folds an included router's middleware into each route before the application sees it. A global middleware may expose `applies_to(method, path)`, consulted once per route at compile time; routes it declines dispatch through a program compiled without it, so declining costs nothing per request. `_select_dispatch` then picks `_handle_http_compartment`, which routes *before* running the tape -- legal only because `classify` needs no Request, and only for an application with a classifying table, no dynamic matcher (host routing matches on a Host `ProxyHeaders` may rewrite) and no stage hooks. Per request it handles only `classify == 1`: a miss, an auth ticket, an armed recorder or an ambiguous path all hand back to `_handle_http` and run the full tape, so a rate limiter still counts 404s. Per-route programs are keyed by `(method, handler)` -- a multi-method route with no route middleware compiles to one shared endpoint object, and method is the axis compartments are most wanted on. `Wreath(middleware="native")` opts into `_middleware_tape`, which records at boot every answer a configured `CORSMiddleware` can give a preflight and lets `_wreath_http` serve them before the tape, before routing and before a `Request` exists. The table is recorded by *asking the middleware*, never by rebuilding its answer beside it -- reconstruction missed the `content-type` a 204 inherits from the Response class default, and the recorded answer must include the middleware's own egress hook, which is where a 403 refusal picks up `access-control-allow-origin` (so refusals are recorded per origin). Each probe runs twice and a middleware whose answers differ is declined. An origin outside the table falls through to Python rather than being refused, because `CORSMiddleware`'s normalized compare accepts spellings the table does not carry. Opting in is a documented ordering change: middleware registered before CORS stops seeing preflights.

subsystems.name: routing
subsystems.capability: Startup-compiled static, parameter, trailing-path and host routing; named reverse lookup; declarative routers; and generic ASGI application mounts
subsystems.policy: Ordinary static and single-segment parameter routes stay on the selected byte-identical pure/native table. Host patterns and a final {name:path} use an ordered startup-compiled Python matcher because the segment-count tables cannot represent either without weakening their hot path: matching host routes run before the ordinary table, while an unscoped trailing-path route is a fallback after that table so it cannot shadow a literal route. Router inclusion remains declarative flattening; Wreath.mount is the explicit request-time ASGI composition surface.

subsystems.name: http
subsystems.capability: Requests and responses, streaming and server-sent events, multipart file uploads, background tasks, and content negotiation over JSON, MessagePack and Protocol Buffers
subsystems.policy: Request.stream is one-shot and enforces max_body_bytes as chunks arrive; body() buffers through that same stream and may be replayed, while consuming stream() first makes later body/json/form reads raise StreamConsumed. Multipart form parsing is incremental and spools a file at the threshold without retaining a whole-request body.

subsystems.name: http-client
subsystems.capability: Outbound HTTP with pooling, rate limiting and retries, service-to-service calls, and signed webhooks in both directions

subsystems.name: binding
subsystems.capability: Typed request and response contracts, rich stdlib scalars, reusable Field constraints and aliases, startup-compiled validation, and dependency injection with Depends
subsystems.policy: Native body validation executes a plan compiled once in Python; binding.validate remains the reference and native must match it byte-for-byte (errors included). Recursive dataclasses and annotations carrying advanced Field/rich-type operations fall back to the pure validator until the native plan can represent the whole contract; a partial native interpretation is forbidden. Supported return annotations filter, validate and serialize plain handler values; explicit Response objects retain wire ownership.

subsystems.name: openapi
subsystems.capability: A strict OpenAPI 3.1 contract derived from runtime validation, explicit responses and security, compatibility comparison, a self-contained docs UI, and generated typed clients
subsystems.policy: Python owns annotation analysis; renderers consume prevalidated tuples and are byte-identical pure/native; generation adds no request-time work; the native renderer is benchmark-gated and currently not justified. OpenAPI refuses unsupported annotations instead of publishing an empty schema. Field metadata, query bounds, primary/additional responses, deprecation, visibility and explicitly registered security schemes render from the same route image. compare_openapi reports stable breaking request/response changes. Docs endpoints are opt-in via enable_docs().

subsystems.name: configuration
subsystems.capability: Environment-driven settings with types and required-variable checks, kept separate from runtime state
subsystems.policy: Environment is an immutable string snapshot. Environment.bind constructs an ordinary dataclass once at startup, converts supported stdlib/enums/literals/unions/containers, recurses into nested groups using double-underscore keys, and raises one SettingsError containing every missing or invalid key. Env supplies an absolute alias, Secret redacts implicit formatting, and source() reports the winning process or dotenv source.

subsystems.name: middleware
subsystems.capability: Rate limiting, CORS, CSRF, sessions, security headers, compression, request IDs, idempotency keys, and cache-control policy
subsystems.policy: Hooks are fused into a linear tape; global middleware (`global_scope = True`) runs around routing and every response, including misses and error responses, so its `after` still runs when a handler raises. Idempotency is *response replay*, not the effect-once guarantee: `IdempotencyMiddleware`'s claim must be atomic (`MemoryIdempotencyStore` is sync between read and write; `PostgresIdempotencyStore` is one INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... RETURNING, where a returned row *is* the claim -- no owner column). The default store is per-worker, so the durable guarantee has to come from a unique index on the key (`jobs.enqueue(key=...)`, a unique column); design so that losing the store costs work, never correctness. `docs/cookbook/recipes/exactly-once.md` and `tests/test_exactly_once.py` hold that composition. Rate limiting has two shapes for one reason: `request.identity` is set during route authorization, so a limiter keyed on the principal cannot be a global hook. `RateLimitMiddleware` stays global and keyed on the address (ingress: 404 floods, login floods) and *raises at construction* if handed `principal_key`, because degrading silently to one shared bucket is a production incident. `TieredRateLimitMiddleware` is route middleware (`global_scope = False`), keyed on the principal, with one store per tier so a promotion gets a full allowance; the tier comes from the caller's roles -- the same roles Cedar authorizes with -- and the most generous match wins. The claim, the lazy statement preparation, the `clock_timestamp()` clock and the offered-not-applied schema live once, in `wreath.store`; a returned row *is* the claim, and `live`/`expired` are exact complements so a purge can never drop a row a read would still honour. `MemoryRateLimitStore` stays outside it deliberately: a token bucket is arithmetic every read advances, not a stored payload. `PostgresSessionStore.delete_for` is the only method that reads inside a session payload, so it is the only one that has to know which key holds the principal: `session_key=` at construction, overridable per call, bound as `$2::text` rather than interpolated so one prepared statement serves every key and an application string never reaches SQL. It was hardcoded to `principal`, so a deployment on `user_router(session_key=...)` got a password reset that matched no row, ended no sessions, and reported success.

subsystems.name: auth
subsystems.capability: Authentication (JWT, API keys, OAuth2 and OIDC login) and authorization on a built-in Cedar policy engine
subsystems.policy: Authentication (identity) and authorization (roles, permissions, Cedar) stay firmly apart. Step-up is the one thing that spans them and lives on the authentication side: `AuthRequirement.second_factor` is a *window*, not a flag, `wreath.auth.second_factor(max_age=...)` sets it, `requirements.second_factor_age` reads `Identity.claims['second_factor_at']` and returns None (a refusal, never a zero) when there is no stamp, merging takes the strictest window, and the Cedar context omits `second_factor_age` entirely rather than faking one so `when`/`has` and `unless`/`has` policies both fail closed. The Cedar engine is built in and dependency-free: policies parse at startup, evaluation is native with a pure twin, forbid overrides permit, default deny. `permissions_router(app)` answers what the caller may do from the *same* authorizer that enforces it, and `declared_actions(app)` reads the vocabulary off the routes' `@authorize` declarations -- there is no second list to drift, and an undeclared action is refused rather than evaluated (otherwise the endpoint is an oracle for probing policies). Two questions, two shapes: the manifest is resource-type level and ETagged (the tag covers principal, roles, and the policy set, so a promotion or a deploy invalidates it and nothing else does); the batch endpoint is row level, because a Cedar decision depends on the resource. Neither is enforcement -- the route is re-evaluated on the next request, so a stale answer can only draw a button that then 403s. The vocabulary reaches the generated TS client through `ApiModel.permissions`. The permission change stream (`_livedoc.LiveDocument`, transported by `_busbridge`) is **at-most-once and advisory**: a narrowing change may arrive late, which is safe only because the manifest is for chrome and enforcement is re-evaluated on the route -- a stale manifest can draw a button that then 403s and can never permit anything. A stream never emits an ETag it cannot state truthfully: on a roles change the captured identity is stale by definition, so it emits `etag: null` rather than a tag that would tell the client to skip exactly the refetch it needs, and coalescing two pending changes lets *unknown* win. Subscriptions are capped per principal and overall and **refused** (503, client falls back to If-None-Match) rather than evicted, since evicting the oldest tab invites a reconnect that evicts the next; the ORM write subscription is registered on the first subscriber and dropped on the last, so the process-global listener list is bounded by live streams. All three discovered OIDC endpoints are pinned to the issuer origin. `jwks_uri` and `token_endpoint` go through `_same_origin_path`, which reduces them to the path their origin-pinned client takes; `authorization_endpoint` is a **browser redirect target**, so it goes through `_require_same_origin` -- the same comparison, returning the URL unchanged -- inside `discover()`, and stays absolute. Reducing it to a path would send every sign-in to this application's own `/authorize`. The check is at discovery rather than at the redirect because the attribute is public and any application may build its own redirect from it; a second check at the use site could never fire and would be a check with nothing to check.

subsystems.name: users
subsystems.capability: Registration, login, email verification, password reset, scrypt password hashing, and second factors: TOTP with hashed recovery codes, and WebAuthn passkeys
subsystems.policy: Second factors, stages one and two of docs/plans/second-factors-totp-webauthn.md: a TOTP code that verified once never verifies again (verify_totp requires a counter strictly greater than the credential's stored one, and SecondFactorStore.touch is an atomic conditional advance that reports whether it won -- one statement with WHERE counter < $1 in OrmSecondFactorStore, a compare-and-set in a synchronous function in InMemorySecondFactorStore -- so a lost advance is refused as a replay and two concurrent requests carrying one code cannot both complete); skew is one step by default and never more than _secondfactor.MAX_SKEW; enrolment is two-phase, so begin_totp_enrolment writes nothing and only a verified code creates a credential, and the unconfirmed secret lives in the `enrolments` SessionStore under an opaque id when one is passed, bound to the user who began it; recovery codes are a single SHA-256 (hash_recovery_code) rather than the password hasher -- ~78 bits needs no slow KDF, passwords still get scrypt -- shown once, compared with hmac.compare_digest, and deleted when redeemed -- the deletion claimed through the same conditional advance the TOTP branch uses, since a remove() that returns nothing cannot say which of two simultaneous redemptions spent the code, with stage one's scrypt$ rows still verifying; a login awaiting a second factor writes a pending marker and never a principal, so SessionIdentityBackend yields no identity for it; verification (promotion or step-up) rotates the session and stamps second_factor_at, which AuthRequirement.second_factor / wreath.auth.second_factor and the Cedar context's second_factor_age read, absent always meaning refused rather than fresh; DELETE /auth/2fa/{id} needs a factor within step_up_ttl, is owner-scoped, refuses a recovery id, and takes the recovery codes with the last real factor; the credential material column is named secret_material because crud.SENSITIVE_FIELD matches that and not `material`. Stage three adds WebAuthn as a second factor, all Python and no new C: _webauthn.py parses CBOR/COSE/authenticator data/DER and delegates every signature to _auth/_ecverify (ES256 and Ed25519 only -- RS256 is refused by name rather than implemented), the parsers refuse indefinite-length CBOR, tags, floats, duplicate keys, trailing bytes, non-minimal DER integers and off-curve points, and only `none` attestation is accepted because verifying an attestation statement needs a metadata service; a ceremony's type, challenge, origin and RP ID hash are four separate refusals; the challenge lives in a ChallengeStore (wreath.store's Keyed primitive, MemoryChallengeStore by default and PostgresChallengeStore for a fleet) rather than in the session, and is spent by one DELETE ... WHERE handle AND user_id AND kind AND expires > clock_timestamp() RETURNING payload -- so the returned row *is* the consumption (two concurrent completions cannot both proceed) and the user binding is a WHERE clause rather than a check after the row is already gone (a mismatched attempt matches no row, deletes nothing, and costs the rightful user nothing). The candidate subject is derived from the session -- a pending login first, then the signed-in principal -- and passed to that statement as a precondition, never read back out of the record, because a record that names its own owner lets whoever holds a handle define who they are; ChallengeStore.peek is a non-consuming read used by the TOTP enrolment path (whose property is confirmed-exactly-once, not read-exactly-once: a mistyped code must not cost a fresh QR scan) and, after a consume has already refused, to choose between ceremony_expired and the binding refusal -- it applies no binding and no security decision rests on it; a signature counter that fails to increase above a stored non-zero one is refused as a clone signal while an authenticator that always reports 0 keeps working; user verification is requested (not required) and its outcome is recorded on the session as second_factor_uv; the webauthn routes mount only when second_factor_router is given rp_id. The accepted origins default to https://{rp_id} and widen for exactly one case: _webauthn.default_origins admits http:// as well when rp_id is a loopback host (localhost, ::1, 127.0.0.0/8), and _webauthn.origin_accepted lets a loopback origin carry any port, since http://localhost:8000 is a secure context and no default set can enumerate a development port -- no other host is ever admitted over http, no port is tolerated off loopback, and there is no wildcard. Building second_factor_router without enrolments= no longer warns, because it no longer degrades: ceremony state goes to a ChallengeStore whose default is real, so the single-use property holds unconditionally instead of being announced as absent. The removed UserWarning could only ever name half its condition -- a router built before any application exists cannot observe whether SessionMiddleware was given a store= -- and a warning nobody can act on with certainty is one people learn to ignore. One behaviour change comes with it, for multi-worker deployments on cookie sessions with no store named: a ceremony is now confined to the worker that began it, which fails closed (refused, begin again) and is what challenges=PostgresChallengeStore answers. The webauthn suite's authenticator is synthetic (a real key and a real signature from cryptography, a dev/test dependency), which proves agreement about the wire formats and not interoperability; interoperability is pinned by one recorded registration and one recorded assertion transcribed from the W3C WebAuthn Level 3 specification's own section 16.2 test vectors (CR Snapshot, 26 May 2026), cited in place -- do not replace those with generated bytes. The two routers are separate but not independent: second_factor_router records itself against the UserStore it was built with, so a user_router over that same store with no second_factors= of its own refuses (500 second_factor_not_wired, no session written) the login of a user who has a non-recovery factor, rather than issuing a password-only sign-in -- and the same refusal covers the other half-wiring, a user_router given a SecondFactorStore that is not the object second_factor_router writes to, which otherwise read an empty store and signed the caller in; and user_router's login and logout both clear pending_totp_enrolment and pending_webauthn from the session and delete the rows behind them, so a ceremony does not outlive the sitting it began in. Every one of those checks is a raise, never an assert. `user_router` hands its own `session_key` to `sessions.delete_for` when it is not the default, so a password reset enumerates by the key login actually wrote the principal under; the default call shape is unchanged so a store written against the one-argument signature keeps working.

subsystems.name: postgres
subsystems.capability: A native PostgreSQL driver: connection pooling, prepared statements, parameter type inference, and COPY
subsystems.policy: Connection.map/Statement.map run one Sync-delimited operation per input in input order (no coalescing/dedup); Connection.transaction() orders reads before dependent writes and discards a connection whose synchronization cannot be proven.

subsystems.name: locks
subsystems.capability: Cluster-wide mutexes and run-once leases, on PostgreSQL advisory locks rather than a second datastore
subsystems.policy: Advisory locks and SingletonRunner are reached through the wreath.postgres facade, not imported from _locks directly.

subsystems.name: orm
subsystems.capability: An async ORM with explicit loading, first-class JSONB and array columns, vector similarity and full-text search without a second datastore, transactions, and tenant-scoped sessions
subsystems.policy:
The dependency direction is one-way: wreath.orm imports wreath.postgres, never the reverse. Attribute access never performs I/O; loading is explicit (no lazy N+1). Pure and native storage must match behavior, not representation; the native query cache-key (orm_shape) must produce bytes identical to _shape_of_pure or the plan cache splits. An extension type's OID is assigned by CREATE EXTENSION and so differs between databases: it is resolved once at startup (orm/introspection.resolve_extension_types) and must never reach a plan-cache shape token or a model fingerprint, both of which are name-derived instead. ColumnSpec.oid reads through the type rather than snapshotting it, and native model storage -- which does bake the OID in at class definition -- is written back by rebind_storage_oid at the same moment. An ORDER BY key that is not a bare column (a vector distance) takes the pure keyer deliberately, because orm_shape.c reads ordering.expression.column. A generated column (`TsVector`) is the database's to write, never the application's: its expression names other columns, so it is rendered by orm/_generated.py once the registry knows their names and types, in PostgreSQL's own deparsed normal form -- a spelling that differs by one byte reports the column as drifted on every migration run, forever.

**Wreath implements the client half of pgvector, never the server half.** The wire codec is ours -- `_pure/postgres.py` and `_native/postgres/codec.c` -- so no `pgvector` Python package is needed and `replaces` lists it for that reason. The `vector`/`halfvec` *types*, the `<->`/`<=>`/`<#>`/`<+>` operators and the HNSW/IVFFlat access methods are extension code inside PostgreSQL; `CREATE EXTENSION vector` is required and no client driver can substitute for it, because an index access method cannot be defined from outside the server. Migrations deliberately never emit `CREATE EXTENSION` (the privilege is usually not the runner's) and `doctor.check_extension_types` is the pre-flight.

**`halfvec` is a second codec kind, not a variant of the first.** `EXT_KIND_VECTOR = 1` frames float4 elements and `EXT_KIND_HALFVEC = 2` frames float2; one OID must never mean two wire formats, since decoding one as the other yields a plausible vector of the wrong length. Adding a kind means a branch in *both* twins at all six dispatch sites (text/binary x encode/decode, plus the two `_decode_value` entry points) -- a missed site silently returns raw bytes, which is how this one was caught. The text form is shared: pgvector prints both types as `[1,2,3]`. Elements are bounded by binary16's largest finite value (65504, `MAX_HALF_MAGNITUDE`) at coercion *and* at encode, because a larger value rounds to an infinity pgvector then refuses. `Halfvec`'s `extension` is `"vector"`, not `"halfvec"` -- one extension provides both, and naming the type would send readers to install something nonexistent. Operator classes are per type (`halfvec_cosine_ops`).

**`sparsevec` is a third kind (`EXT_KIND_SPARSEVEC = 3`) and `bit` is not an extension type at all.** The same six-dispatch-site rule applies to `sparsevec`, plus a seventh consideration the first two did not have: its Python value is neither a list nor anything else a builtin can express, so `wreath._sparsevec.SparseVector` carries the dimension and the index-to-value mapping together. That module holds one class and imports nothing from wreath, because *both* codec twins need it -- `_pure/postgres.py` imports it directly and `codec.c` resolves it in module init beside `uuid.UUID`. Its validation is not restated in C: two copies of a bounds check are two chances to disagree about what pgvector accepts, and the sparse paths are cold. **`SparseVector` counts indices from 1** (pgvector's text form and its documentation do) while the binary wire counts from 0; the conversion lives in `_encode_sparsevec`/`_decode_sparsevec` and their C twins and nowhere else. It carries `_pg_oid` on a *copy* made by `to_wire`, for the same parameter-inference reason `WireList` exists, because the caller's own value may outlive the bind and be bound against another database.

**`Bit` is PostgreSQL's own `bit`, OID 1560 -- a compile-time constant with no resolution step.** Only pgvector's `<~>` (hamming) and `<%>` (jaccard) operators over it, and the `bit_hamming_ops`/`bit_jaccard_ops` index classes, come from the extension, which is why `_bit_distance` gates on the OID rather than on `isinstance(pg_type, ExtensionType)`. The wire format packs bits MSB-first with the final byte padded on the right; reversed, every value still round-trips through the codec and every distance the server computes is wrong, so `tests/orm/test_bit_codec.py` asserts the packing against literal bytes rather than only through a round trip. Non-zero padding is refused rather than masked away, because masking would make two wire values decode to one string.

**A halfvec value's decimal depends on the result format**: the binary decoder widens the stored binary16 exactly (`0.0999755859375`), pgvector's text rendering prints nine significant digits (`0.099975586`). Different Python floats. Pinned in `tests/orm/test_halfvec_live.py`.

subsystems.name: series
subsystems.capability: Chart data as a declaration: buckets, fills, and rankings computed in the database in the reader's own timezone
subsystems.policy: Chart data as a declaration over one source model, with a bounded result. Bucketing is a timezone problem before it is an aggregation problem: the bucket is assigned and the spine generated on the local wall clock, then converted back, because generate_series stepping naive timestamps advances a calendar day while stepping timestamptz advances exactly 24 hours -- the DST bug, twice a year, in one bucket. Ranges are half-open and stated once, for the filter and the spine bounds alike. Fill is per measure: count and sum fill with 0, avg/min/max stay null, because an average of no rows is undefined and drawing it as zero reads as a collapse rather than an absence. A series is identified by a stable key from the grouping value, never by rank, so a filter change cannot repaint a legend. Multiple measures are multiple named series and are never merged -- two units on one pair of axes is a dual-axis chart, whose alignment is arbitrary. Top-N folds (it preserves the total) and the fold is applied before aggregation, so the remainder's average is a real average and not an average of averages; every other ceiling refuses rather than truncating. Not plan-cached, following compile_count: a declaration runs once per chart request, not once per row. Bucket vocabulary lives in wreath.temporal because sealing will need end_of() too.

subsystems.name: infra
subsystems.capability: Infrastructure inferred from an application's own declarations: databases, object stores, egress, and the environment contract it needs supplied
subsystems.policy: Stage 1 is read-only: `wreath infra infer` derives a typed plan from the objects an application's declarations built, and never imports a cloud SDK, opens a socket, writes state, or applies anything -- both properties are asserted by tests. Inference walks the registries itself rather than calling Wreath._components_by_database, because that lookup misses JobRunner._db and a middleware's _store. A settings dataclass named with --settings is turned into the keys Environment.bind will read and checked against --env/--environ; a required key with no supplier is a gap and the command exits 1. Subsystems needing no new infrastructure are listed as such, including the ones the application does not use, because the absence of a broker is the finding. Declaring resources, emitting Terraform JSON, diffing live state, and applying are later stages and are not shipped.

subsystems.name: migrations
subsystems.capability: Schema diffing, migration artifacts, apply, and a derived inverse that refuses to strand live code
subsystems.policy: Readiness resolution is metal-only. The inverse `down` is derived from the same artifact as the forward migration and refuses to strand live ORM code unless --force. Single-schema `apply` ships; applying one artifact across a fleet of tenant schemas is still unshipped, as tracked in docs/reference/roadmap.md. A deferred migration declares its conversion beside the model rather than in a migration file, because artifacts are generated from the catalog and there is nothing to decorate. `Recode` (same type, new values) is guarded by a predicate scan that refuses ordered comparison, patterns, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY` and joins on a converting column; `Retype` (new type, two columns) is guarded by the gate instead, because an unconverted row reads NULL rather than reading wrong. Refusal is the default: a false refusal costs an argument, a false permission costs a silent incident. A scan that examined nothing refuses rather than reporting clean. **A column's SQL type is reconstructed from its OID, and two kinds of type cannot be.** `migration_sql.c::sql_type_for_oid` maps a built-in OID to its spelling and a type missing from that switch does not fail loudly: it renders as an *empty* `MANUAL` statement, so `generate` omits the column and then emits the constraints and indexes that reference it, and applying the plan fails on a column that was never added. `json`, `character varying` and `bit(n)` were all missing this way, which is why tests/migrations/test_object_coverage.py now enumerates every built-in `PgType` in `__all__` rather than the ones somebody thought of. The second kind is a type whose *modifier* is part of it: `bit(8)` and `bit(512)` share OID 1560, so the OID alone loses the width. Those spell themselves in the descriptor exactly as an extension type does, and the set is written twice -- `migrations._MODIFIER_BEARING_OIDS` and a hard-coded `<> 1560` in `_SINGLE_CATALOG_SQL`, because a CASE cannot read a frozenset. **Both sides must produce the identical string or the column is rediscovered as drift on every run forever**, which is the same silent failure the vector default-opclass defect had; test_catalog_integration.py holds them equal against a real catalog.

subsystems.name: jobs
subsystems.capability: Durable Postgres-backed jobs and schedules, pub/sub messaging, WebSocket rooms, task progress, and supervised background services
subsystems.policy: PostgreSQL is the queue; there is no broker to operate. The service supervisor starts after databases and before user startup handlers, and stops in reverse: stop fetching, drain bounded in-flight work, then cancel. Watchable work: `JobRunner(progress=ProgressRegistry(...))` makes the job id the task id -- one identifier, no correlation -- and `launch()` seeds it `queued` so a client polling before a worker claims it does not get a 404. The runner owns the terminal states because only it can tell a retry from a dead-letter: success reports `done`, dead-letter reports `failed` with the error, and a retry leaves the task `running`. A handler never reports terminal state itself. `ProgressRegistry(bus)` carries reports to every worker on one channel with the rooms.py origin guard (apply locally, publish once, never relay what arrived); at-most-once, and a bus failure cannot fail the work being reported on. Cross-worker transport discipline is one primitive: `_busbridge.BusBridge` owns the channel, the origin tag that drops a worker's own NOTIFY echo, and the deferred publish, and there is deliberately **no path from its receive to a publish** -- never-relaying is structural, not a flag. `rooms.py`, `progress.py`, and `_orm_events.WriteBroadcast` each keep only their payload shape and local apply. The one real difference is preserved: rooms publishes inline and unsuppressed (its caller is awaiting the fan-out), the other two are fire-and-forget and swallow (the row already committed; a percentage is commentary). Durable subscriber groups are discovered fleet-wide from a `message_groups` table, **unioned** with local registrations so a missing table degrades to the old behaviour and shipping before the DDL cannot regress; the snapshot is refreshed on a timer (`group_refresh`, 30s) rather than read per publish, because a query inside the caller's `tx` would abort *their* transaction if the table were absent. Registry failures are counted (`group_registry_errors`), never raised. A publish routed to nobody stays a no-op but increments `unrouted_publishes`; `require_group=True` raises `NoSubscriberGroup` instead. The doorbell's held LISTEN connection is supervised: it reconnects with jittered exponential backoff (50 ms to 5 s, no reset for a connection that flaps), counts losses and failed opens in `doorbell_reconnects`, and counts ephemeral handler exceptions separately in `handler_errors` so a bug in user code cannot read as a dropped connection. A handler is cancelled at `deadline_for(task)` -- `task(timeout=...)`, defaulting to `DEADLINE_FRACTION` (0.8) of the lease, and refused at registration if it is not shorter than the lease. There is no heartbeat, so a handler still running when its lease expires is reclaimed and run again by another worker: the fence stops the loser's bookkeeping landing, never the duplicate side effect. `drive()` passes a pass's own `shift` as its deadline rather than taking the default, because that bound is already declared and already checked. A cancelled handler charges an attempt and retries (a deadline miss is usually a slow dependency) and counts in `run_timeouts`, apart from `run_errors`: nothing failed, work was stopped.

subsystems.name: workflows
subsystems.capability: Durable multi-step sagas: ordered steps whose results are recorded before the next starts, resume from the first unrecorded step, and compensation newest-first when one raises
subsystems.policy:
**A completed step never runs twice.** Each step's return value is recorded before the next one starts, so `resume` re-enters at the first step with no record and reads the *recorded* result rather than recomputing it. That is the whole difference from a loop over callables.

**Compensation runs newest-first, and the step that raised is not compensated** -- it never completed, so there is nothing of its to undo, and an undo against state that was never established turns a recoverable failure into a corrupt one.

**A compensation that raises is counted, not swallowed** (AGENTS.md's third tier: broad catch, counted, waived in place with a reason). The undos behind a failed one still run, or the saga is left more broken than if nothing had been undone. The count is durable on the instance and read with `Workflow.status`, because a run that compensates re-raises the step's own exception -- so the summary cannot come back as a return value, and a half-compensated saga has to be findable later by someone without the traceback.

**Renaming a step of a live instance raises `WorkflowDefinitionChanged`.** Completion is keyed on the step *name*, so a rename leaves a record matching nothing and a naive resume redoes completed work and reports success. The stored step list is written at `begin` for exactly this comparison. This is the one failure here that would otherwise be invisible.

`PostgresWorkflowStore` keeps its two tables in a dedicated system schema with a `tenant` column and never relies on `search_path`, which is `jobs`'s rule for the same reason. Its resume path is covered against a live server by `tests/test_workflows_checklist.py::test_postgres_store_survives_a_crash_between_steps` (marked `network`, gated on `WREATH_TEST_POSTGRES_DSN`), because the in-memory store satisfies the resume contract only within one process -- precisely not the situation sagas exist for.

subsystems.name: passes
subsystems.capability: Backfills, rollups, and reindexes as a durable, resumable, paced walk over a big table
subsystems.policy: A pass converts the past; the application writes the future in the shape the pass is converting to. That precondition is the primitive's rule rather than a caller's choice, and it is what makes a fixed ceiling sound. The cursor advances inside the chunk transaction, so position and data commit together -- the whole reason this is worth owning is that the ledger row and the walked table are two rows in one PostgreSQL cluster. The compare-and-swap is the chunk's first statement: it takes the row lock, so two workers serialise and the loser rolls back whole rather than doing anything observable. That exclusivity argument is why parallel sharded execution is deliberately not planned. The vocabulary is 'a half-open range over one ordered domain'; row counts are reported, never structural, so a bucketed range source still fits. Keyset never OFFSET is a complexity argument (N^2/(2c) against (N/c)*log N + N) and needs no benchmark -- its two correctness conditions are refusals: the leading key column must be indexed, and a composite key is one row comparison, never expanded ORs. A boundary that cannot be proven unique is refused because '>' silently skips siblings and '>=' loops forever. Pacing ships in the first release rather than after it: the primitive must not have a version in which an unpaced walk exists.

subsystems.name: objects
subsystems.capability: Object storage over S3-compatible services or local disk, with presigned uploads and downloads
subsystems.policy: Blob/object storage: the `ObjectStore` protocol with `MemoryObjectStore` (the dev/test twin), a symlink-safe `LocalObjectStore` on the same `openat` containment as static files, and `S3ObjectStore` over `http_client` signed with zero-dependency SigV4. `normalize_key` is the single containment gate for every backend -- a key is validated there, not per backend. Named `objects` because "store" meant two unrelated things: this, and the small keyed tables behind rate limiting, idempotency, and sessions (`wreath.store`). `src/wreath/storage.py` is a deprecating alias that re-exports the old names (`Storage`/`S3Storage`/`StoragePath`/`StorageError`) and warns; it exists so the rename cannot break an existing import, and is removable once callers have moved.

subsystems.name: grpc
subsystems.capability: Serve gRPC methods over the native HTTP/2 server, declared as routes so one authorization vocabulary covers REST and gRPC alike
subsystems.policy: A gRPC method is a *route*, registered as `POST /{service}/{method}` on an ordinary `Router`. That is not a convenience: it is what makes `@roles`, `@authorize`, `permissions=` and `dependencies=` mean the same thing here as on a REST route, enforced by the same tape and read by `permissions_router` and `wreath mutant` from the same place -- there is no second authorization model to drift. The route registers a *wrapper* around the user's function, so `GrpcService.router` copies the `AuthRequirement` the auth decorators recorded on their function onto the wrapper; without that copy a `@roles` on a gRPC method would read as enforcement and enforce nothing, which is precisely the unwatched control the mutation tester exists to find. `_GrpcResponse` subclasses `StreamingResponse` because the application's return-value coercion is a closed isinstance check over four response types -- duck-typing `__call__(send)` is not enough -- and inheriting also picks up the deferred-cleanup contract that releases a borrowed database connection. It drives `http.response.start(trailers=True)`, bodies, then `http.response.trailers` itself, which is the only path to the ASGI trailers extension: the native HTTP/2 server implements it in C and nothing else in `wreath.response` ever sends those messages. The HTTP status is always 200, including for a refusal, because in gRPC the transport succeeded whenever the server was reached and the outcome is the `grpc-status` trailer; a handler that fails after its first message is already on the wire reports its status there rather than re-raising, since re-raising aborts the stream with no status and a client reads that as an unexplained transport error instead of the refusal it was. An unrecognised exception maps to UNKNOWN and never to UNAVAILABLE or ABORTED, both of which tell a client to retry. The four-byte length prefix is attacker-controlled and is checked against `max_message_bytes` before anything is allocated. Two transport constraints come from the server and not from here: gRPC needs response trailers, which only wreath's own server emits, and wreath negotiates h2 through ALPN and never sniffs the first application bytes, so prior-knowledge h2c is unavailable and gRPC requires TLS. **ASGI offers no way to learn at startup which protocols the server will speak**, so the refusal for a foreign server is the first thing every call does rather than a startup check. Server reflection is not built and is coupled to `wreath.protobuf` deliberately not building descriptors; a gRPC *client* is not built because `http_client` has no HTTP/2 at all.

subsystems.name: mcp
subsystems.capability: A Model Context Protocol server: declared Python callables served to a model as tools, resources and prompts, over streamable HTTP
subsystems.policy: Stages 1-4 of `docs/plans/native-mcp-server.md`: `initialize`, `ping`, `tools/*`, `resources/*`, `prompts/*` and `notifications/cancelled` over streamable HTTP, the `GET` server-to-client stream, `expose_routes`, plus the whole authorization boundary. **No new C, at any stage** -- the plan decided this: the JSON-RPC envelope is `_native/json.c`, SSE framing is `_native/sse.c` via `SSEResponse`, ingress and routing are the ordinary native path, token verification rides `jose.c` through `JwtVerifier`, authorization rides `cedar.c` through `CedarAuthorizer`, and what is left is startup-time registration plus once-per-call orchestration. A tool's `inputSchema` is derived from `binding.inspect_handler` and rendered by `openapi._openapi_schema`/`_component_schema`, differing from the OpenAPI document only in the `$ref` base (`#/$defs/` against `#/components/schemas/`); `tests/test_mcp_schema.py` pins that parity and is the reason there is no second validator. The stage-1 optimization is Python and is the cached `tools/list` bytes -- `ToolRegistry.listing()` serializes once and registration invalidates it. A binding source a call cannot fill (header, cookie, form field, upload, path placeholder, `Depends`) is refused at registration, not at call time. **Five outcomes stay distinguishable**, for the reason `messaging.MessageBus` separates `doorbell_reconnects` from `handler_errors`: `ToolError` is a *result* carrying `isError`; an unplanned exception is caught at the boundary, counted in `tool_errors`, and reports only its type; arguments that miss the schema never reach the tool and count in `schema_rejections`; a Cedar denial counts in `unauthorized_calls`; a rate-limit or concurrency refusal counts in `throttled`. `MCP.stats()` returns those counters plus `expired_sessions` by name, the shape `MessageBus.stats()` uses; the plan expected the OTLP/Prometheus/StatsD bridges to carry them for free and they do not -- every bridge renders `Projector.snapshot()`'s per-route aggregates and never discovers a subsystem's own counters -- so publishing them is a route the deployment mounts and gates itself. Each outcome also names itself on the per-call Flight Recorder marker (`_mcp/record.py`), which is emitted through `wreath.logging` -- the site is re-interned when the installed runtime's registry moves, because a site interned at import belongs to whichever registry was installed then. Argument *values* follow `wreath.logging`'s deny-by-default rule and argument *names* follow `crud.SENSITIVE_FIELD`; there is no MCP-specific redaction code and there must not be. `MCPAuth` (`_mcp/auth.py`) serves RFC 9728 metadata at `metadata_path_for(path)` -- the well-known segment is *inserted before* the endpoint path, not appended -- reuses `_auth/oauth2.bearer_challenge` (extended, never duplicated) for the RFC 6750 challenge, and performs the `aud` check itself rather than trusting the verifier's `audience=`, because a misconfigured verifier has no symptom until it is exploited. Sessions are bound to the subject that opened them and expire on idle (`MCPLimits.session_idle_seconds`), swept on touch rather than by a background task. **The binding is resolved through whichever of the two ways in identified the caller**, and read that way on every later message: it used to record only the identity `MCPAuth` had published, so an application authenticating with its own `app.configure_auth(...)` backend -- the supported second way, and the one `expose_routes` exists for -- opened every session with `principal=None` and bound nothing, which made a leaked `Mcp-Session-Id` a credential another verified caller could drive that session's calls, `DELETE` and notification stream with. `MCP._initialize` therefore falls back to `_identify` when `MCPAuth` published nobody, and `MCP._owns` resolves the same way when the session it is checking *is* bound; an endpoint with neither has nobody to bind to and its sessions stay open to whoever holds the id, which is stated in the guide rather than left to be discovered (`tests/test_red_team_mcp.py`). Payload size is deliberately *not* in `MCPLimits`: it is `RequestLimits.max_body_bytes`, and a second ceiling would be a second place to forget. The legacy two-endpoint HTTP+SSE transport is out of scope permanently. **`GET` now opens the session's notification stream** (it answered 405 through stage 2, deliberately, because there was nothing to send): one per session, a second is 409, the queue is bounded by `MCPLimits.max_pending_notifications` and a drop is counted in `notifications_dropped` rather than swallowed, the close sentinel evicts the oldest to guarantee delivery, and the generator emits an SSE comment every `stream_keepalive_seconds` because nothing in `SSEResponse` is on a timer. **Progress is `wreath.progress` relayed, never a second mechanism**: `ToolContext.progress` is an ordinary `ProgressReporter` on a `ProgressRegistry` the deployment may supply (a bus-backed one makes it fleet-wide), a watcher task polls `ProgressRegistry.stream` only when the call carried `_meta.progressToken`, and the entry is seeded at 0% first because `stream` gives up on a task id that never appears. A resource is gated on **its own URI** as the Cedar resource and a prompt on its own name, because both have a stable identity and a tool does not. Prompt arguments are refused at registration unless they are strings, since MCP carries them as a string map. **`Tool.policy` became `Tool.requirement: AuthRequirement`** so `expose_routes` can hand a route's merged requirement (`definition.requirement` + `requirement_for(endpoint)`) through unchanged -- authenticated, second factor, roles, permissions and policies are all enforced in `MCP._authorize`, and `_identify` falls back to the app's own auth backend so a route protected by a session backend still works. **That fallback runs before the rate limit is charged and before the audit marker is written**, not after: `_tools_call` (and `_sampling`/`_elicit` for a gate declared only on `sampling=`/`elicitation=`) calls `_identify` whenever the tool has a limiter or a non-zero `access_level`. It used to run only inside `_authorize`, so on an endpoint with no `MCPAuth` a per-tool ceiling keyed on the session was reset by a free `initialize` (1/hour admitted 6 calls) and the marker said `anonymous` for a caller the same request authorized as `User::ada`. The laziness is the point of the condition: an ungated, unbounded tool still never runs the backend; exposing a route must never be a hole around what was in front of it. `expose_routes` takes `tags=`/`include=`/`predicate=` and **has no `all=True`, permanently**; it refuses a route with no docstring and one whose signature a call cannot fill, naming the route as well as the parameter (`derive_input_schema` is passed the route path precisely so a placeholder is classified and refused rather than becoming an argument). **It also refuses a route carrying its own `middleware=` or `dependencies=`**, because a tool invokes the handler and does not replay the route's chain: those two are controls somebody put on that route -- a `before` hook returning a `403`, a `Depends(require_api_key)` that raises -- and carrying `definition.requirement` while dropping them silently published the handler to a model with strictly less in front of it than the HTTP path had. Refusing is ADR 0019's answer and leaves running them later open where admitting the call would not; application middleware from `app.add_middleware(...)` is not in `definition.middleware` and already covers the endpoint, so nothing is refused for a control it still has (`tests/test_red_team_mcp.py`). **Error codes were renumbered once**: `-32002` is now the specification's own `RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND`, and Wreath's `RATE_LIMITED`/`TOO_MANY_CALLS` moved to `-32003`/`-32004` -- the collision was real, since the resources chapter names -32002 and clients special-case it. **Stage 4 shipped sampling, elicitation, roots, completions and the stdio wrapper, and every one of them reuses rather than adds.** The new machinery is `_mcp/outbound.py`: server-to-client *requests* need correlation, which stage 3's `GET` stream did not carry, so a `ClientChannel` per session holds a bounded pending table (`MCPLimits.max_pending_requests`) keyed on ids prefixed `wreath-` (JSON-RPC gives each direction its own id space). `Message` now carries `result`/`error` and `_post` routes a response into that table. **The reentrancy is the sharp edge and it works only because a `tools/call` already runs in its own task**: the answer arrives on a *different* POST while the call is parked, so a design that ran the call inline on the POST's coroutine would deadlock -- `tests/test_mcp_outbound.py` pins that a tool that elicits mid-call completes, a client that never answers times out and is told to stop (`notifications/cancelled` on the withdrawn id), `notifications/cancelled` on the outer call cancels the inner one, and `SessionStore.discard` fails every outstanding future (`ClientChannel.fail_all`, needed because a `resources/read` awaits on the POST's own coroutine and is in nobody's `in_flight`). A capability the client did not advertise in `initialize` is refused before anything is sent, never queued for a client that will not answer. **Sampling is declared per tool** as `Tool.sampling_requirement: AuthRequirement | None` -- None means the tool may not sample, which is the default -- decided by the same `_authorize` over a `_Gate`, spending the tool's *own* `MemoryRateLimitStore` bucket, and recorded at the same `_mcp/record.py` site with `sampled`/`sample_denied`/`sample_throttled`/`sample_failed`. It is in `declared_actions()` too. **Elicitation's requested schema is `derive_input_schema` over a signature synthesized from the form dataclass's fields** (`_mcp/elicit.py`, using `binding._dataclass_spec` so the annotations are the already-resolved objects), and the answer goes through `bind_arguments` -- the same validator, so a bad answer counts in `schema_rejections`; MCP forbids nesting, so a non-primitive property is refused with the field named. The answer is recorded through `record_arguments(prefix=ELICIT_PREFIX)`, so `crud.SENSITIVE_FIELD` hides a `password` a person typed exactly as it hides one a model sent. **Elicitation is gated exactly as sampling is, and this is not optional**: `Tool.elicitation_requirement: AuthRequirement | None` from `@mcp.tool(elicitation="Form::ask")` (or `True` for no policy), None meaning the tool may not prompt at all -- same `_authorize`/`_Gate` decision, same tool rate-limit bucket, same record site with `elicited`/`elicit_declined`/`elicit_denied`/`elicit_throttled`/`elicit_failed`, and in `declared_actions()`. Both declarations are built by one `registry.gate_requirement(...)`, because the bool/action/None handling must not drift apart. The reason is sharper than sampling's and belongs in the guide as well as here: an elicitation renders arbitrary requested fields **inside a client UI the person already trusts**, so a tool asking for `{"password": str}` is a phishing surface wearing that chrome, and "the user is asked and can decline" is precisely the control social engineering defeats -- which is why the earlier no-gate reasoning was wrong and was reversed before release. A resource reader and a prompt handler carry no declaration and so may not prompt either, which is already true of sampling. **Roots are enforced, not listed**: `ToolContext.read_file` opens beneath `MCP(file_root=...)` through `wreath._fsguard` (the walk static files and templates use, refusing symlinks and `..`) on a worker thread, and additionally requires the name to lie beneath a client-declared root -- lexical check on the requested name, descriptor walk on the opened file, and both are needed. A server with no `file_root=` reads nothing; `notifications/roots/list_changed` invalidates the per-session cache. **Completions have no registry**: a prompt argument annotated `Literal`/`Enum` already renders an `enum`, `Prompt.completions` reads it off at build time, and `_is_string_schema` was widened to admit a string enum for exactly that reason. A `ref/resource` completion answers empty, consistently with `resources/templates/list`. **`wreath mcp stdio` is a byte relay, not a second dispatch path**: `_mcp/stdio.py` drives the app through `wreath.testing.TestClient` (lifespan included) and consumes the `GET` stream incrementally via the extracted `TestClient._scope`, because `request()` collects and would never return on an open stream; each inbound line after `initialize` is dispatched as its own task, since awaiting each POST in turn would make the relay unable to read the very line carrying the answer it is waiting for. New counters on `stats()`: `sampling_requests`, `sampling_refusals`, `elicitations`, `elicitation_declines`, `elicitation_refusals`, `client_request_timeouts`, `roots_refusals`. New bounds: `max_pending_requests`, `client_request_seconds`, `max_file_bytes`. A client that POSTs `sampling/createMessage`/`elicitation/create`/`roots/list` is told they go the other way rather than 'unknown method'. Still not built: `logging/setLevel`, stream resumption by `Last-Event-ID`, templated resources and `listChanged`. Dynamic client registration is permanently out of scope -- it is an authorization-server endpoint.

subsystems.name: pagination
subsystems.capability: Page, size, sort, and filter query parameters turned into safe queries over an allow-list of columns
subsystems.policy: Sorting and filtering are allow-list only; apply_sort/apply_filters fall back to sortable_fields(model), which is every column except the retrieval ones (Vector, TsVector). Excluded because pgvector gives vector a btree opclass, so ?sort=embedding is valid SQL that runs -- a full sort on kilobyte values with no index that can serve it, from a query string an anonymous caller controls, i.e. the same request-triggered cost MAX_PAGE bounds twenty lines away. It is a default, not a prohibition: an explicit allow= naming one is still honoured.

subsystems.name: crud
subsystems.capability: Generated REST CRUD routes for an ORM model, off until you opt in twice
subsystems.policy: Generate REST routes from an ORM model, off by default: enabled at the app level (Wreath.enable_crud) and opted into per model (Wreath.crud / crud_router). Sensitive columns (password, *_hash, token, ...) are hidden from output and rejected from input unless named in expose=. Retrieval columns (Vector, TsVector -- `crud.retrieval_fields`, typed rather than name-guessed) are likewise withheld both ways unless named in expose=: an embedding in a response is ~30k floats per default page and a tsvector is derived from columns already in it, while an embedding on input lets anyone who may edit a row top every semantic search without changing visible content. Generated columns (every TsVector) are dropped from input unconditionally, like the primary key, rather than reaching the ORM and answering 422; expose= makes one readable and nothing makes one writable. fields= names what may leave and never widens what may be written. Authorization is per operation via authorize={op|group|'*': Access.*}: Access.roles/permissions/cedar attach AuthRequirement metadata the app enforces in its single-pass pipeline; Access.deny() 403s unconditionally; object_authorizer=(request, op, instance) covers row-level checks that need the loaded row. Single-column primary key only.

subsystems.name: audit
subsystems.capability: An offline accessibility (WCAG 2.1 A/AA) and performance auditor for the HTML and responses your app returns
subsystems.policy: The ruleset is curated and zero-dependency. A new rule is a module under src/wreath/_audit/rules/ registered in that package's __init__, plus a row in docs/reference/audit.md giving its WCAG success criterion or performance budget, its severity, and whether --fix can remediate it. Reached through `wreath audit`, not a public module.

subsystems.name: mutant
subsystems.capability: Mutation testing that removes one *declared control* at a time -- an AuthRequirement field, a Cedar policy, a refusal, a withheld-field filter, a rate limit's key -- and reports the ones no test noticed
subsystems.policy:
A report, not a gate: `wreath mutant` exits 0 and is absent from `wreath-check`, for `wreath-dup-scan`'s reason -- many survivors are legitimate (a defence behind another defence, a branch a deployment cannot reach) and a gate that cries wolf trains everyone to stop reading it. `--fail-on-survivor` opts in, and is meant for a module already cleared.

**Operators name a control, never an operator.** There is no `<` -> `<=`; every mutation is a sentence from a post-mortem (`predicate.drop-operand`, `predicate.always-true`, `expression.take-branch`, `comprehension.drop-clause`, `guard.remove-raise|never-fires|always-fires|drop-statement`, `declaration.drop-keyword|widen-bound`, `cedar.flip-effect|drop-condition|delete-policy`, `value.widen-bound|disable-pattern|empty-denylist`). That scoping is what keeps equivalent mutants rare enough to be honest about, and `tests/test_mutant.py` pins the operator names and their count so one that stops being emitted turns the suite red rather than quietly shrinking coverage (ADR 0024).

**Nothing is written to the tree.** The mutated module is compiled in the parent and the one changed code object is assigned over the live function's `__code__` in the forked child, which every `from x import y` alias sees because they share the function object; an import-time constant has no function to recompile and is rebound by *identity* in the defining module and in every module that imported it. The patch target is the **outermost** enclosing function, not the innermost, because a handler defined inside a router factory has no reachable function object -- recompiling the factory is what makes the next `crud_router(...)` build a mutated handler. The cost of that choice is a real blind spot: a control inside a factory that only ran at import will survive for a reason unrelated to the tests, and the guide says so.

**Test selection is `sys.monitoring` (PEP 669), never `sys.settrace`** -- Wreath is 3.14-only, so it may use the API every cross-version tool is denied. Only lines some operator proposed a mutation for are watched; every other location retires with one `DISABLE`. Measured on this repository: 118.2s instrumented against ~116s uninstrumented over 8,018 tests. A `def` line must never be the watched line for `predicate.always-true` -- it runs once at import, and watching it reported a covered control as UNREACHED, the tool inventing ADR 0024's failure mode for itself.

**A mutant is KILLED only when a test that passed at baseline fails.** An already-failing test can never catch anything and counting it would report safety that is not there. A mutation that cannot be built or applied is ERROR, never SURVIVED: a survivor is read as 'your tests would not notice', and a mutation that never reached the interpreter would say that falsely.

**UNREACHED is reported separately from SURVIVED**, because 'the suite would not notice' and 'the suite never looks' are different problems with different fixes. Equivalence is decided only where it is decidable -- identical bytecode -- and everything else stays undecided rather than being guessed at.

`declaration.drop-keyword` only offers a keyword the callee genuinely defaults, checked against the live signature: a mutant that raises `TypeError` would be caught by any test that ran it, and a broken mutant scored as a catch inflates the report with something the suite did not notice. The `predicate.*`/`guard.*`/`expression.*`/`comprehension.*` operators are confined to functions whose own source names a control (`CONTROL_TOKENS`); that is a heuristic, it is public and importable, and it is why the JSON encoder is not offered for mutation.

The tool was accepted on a two-directional experiment against six exploitable defects fixed on 2026-07-29, each with a regression test written the same day: **specificity** -- all six reported KILLED against the tree as it stands, each by its own regression test -- and **sensitivity** -- in a scratchpad shadow tree (ADR 0023) with that defect's regression tests physically deleted, the same control reported SURVIVED. Re-run it before trusting a change to the operator library or to candidate selection; a mutation tester that cannot detect known-missing coverage is worse than none, because it will be trusted. Linux-first: `os.fork()` is what makes a mutant cost a process rather than a full import graph.

subsystems.name: operations
subsystems.capability: Liveness and readiness checks, feature flags with deterministic percentage rollouts, and API versioning

subsystems.name: observability
subsystems.capability: Structured logging on the flight recorder's ring, metrics and traces bridged to OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, StatsD and CloudWatch, and replay
subsystems.policy: Recording is deny-by-default: `wreath.recording` decides what may be captured, and capture itself ships -- the native recorder arms, triggers, redacts, and writes WFR1 (tests/test_flight_capture_live.py drives an armed forensic request end to end and reads the capture back). The projector drains the recorder's ring off the request path. `replay.generate_test` turns a WTR1 transport recording into a runnable pytest over TestClient: it parses the request out of the recorded bytes (request line + headers + Content-Length body only -- chunked or truncated is refused by name, never guessed), replays it now, and asserts what it observes. That makes it a *characterisation* test, and the generated docstring says so -- generated against a broken build it encodes the bug, generated after the fix it locks the fix in. Host/content-length/connection headers are dropped from the generated call because they are the test client's business, not the behaviour under test. Logging packs a *published* record in C (`Recorder.log`, `_flightmodule.c`) straight into a ring cell; the Python packer beside it is the pure twin of ADR 0005, checked byte for byte and by mismatch count over a corpus (tests/test_logging_native_parity.py), and it is what actually runs in three cases -- no recorder, a buffered record awaiting promotion, and a record made off the loop. The ring has exactly one writer, so an off-loop call is staged and published by the loop one interval later flagged LOG_FLAG_OFF_LOOP; before that existed such a call raced `ring_publish` and corrupted the ring. Every cost here is measured rather than asserted: benchmarks/bench_logging.py runs the six measurements and benchmarks/results/logging_2026-07-28_*.json retains before and after. The measurements found the fast tier was not fast (a pure-Python SipHash on the request path), and the parity corpus found three values that raised out of `pack_value`, which promises never to. The ring is heap memory by default and a MAP_SHARED file when `TelemetryConfig.ring_path` is set, so a process that dies badly leaves its last cells readable (`wreath.recording.read_ring_file`, `wreath flight read`). That is survival of the *process*, never durability: the pages are the kernel's, and only a clean shutdown msyncs. The ring refuses when full rather than overwriting, so a crash file's mirrored RING_FULL counter is what says whether it is the story or a sample of it; the archival EVNT stream in the WFR1 recording holds everything the projector already drained. tests/test_flight_ring_file.py forks a child and kills it with SIGSEGV and SIGKILL rather than simulating a crash, because the single claim the feature rests on is that the records are still there afterwards. A ring file and a WTR1 recording join through the *sequence of log call sites*, not an id -- a transport recording carries none: `replay.reproduce_from_ring` (and `wreath flight replay`) re-drives the recording and reports where the path parts from the one the crash file recorded, exiting 1 on divergence so it works as a check. Site ids are import order, so this is only meaningful against the build that crashed; a divergence at index 0 is the symptom of running it against a different one.

subsystems.name: server
subsystems.capability: A native HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and optional HTTP/3 server, with WebSockets, TLS, and a development runner
subsystems.policy: Framework and server layers stay separable: Wreath must remain usable on any conforming ASGI server. ASGI semantics come before implementation speed.

subsystems.name: reactor
subsystems.capability: An asyncio-compatible event loop for the experimental metal server tier, with inline completion for non-suspending requests and an optional native timing wheel
subsystems.policy: The metal tier's loop. Free-threading and the optional JIT are separately tested execution modes, not assumptions. See tests/reactor/README.md for the tier layout and counter contracts.

subsystems.name: templates
subsystems.capability: A server-side template engine that compiles once at startup and escapes by default
subsystems.policy: Safe HTML templates escape by default (Markup opts out). Parsing/compilation is startup-time Python producing a flat opcode tape; the native engine renders the tape byte-identically to _pure.templates.render_tape and raises the same errors. No arbitrary Python evaluation. A lookup path may not contain a segment starting with `_`, refused in `_parse_path` -- at compile time, which is why the rule needs no native twin: the native engine only executes a tape the pure compiler produced. It is there because a lookup falls back from subscript to `getattr`, so `{{ u.__init__.__globals__.API_KEY }}` read a module global into the output; with no call opcode the ceiling was disclosure, not execution, but it was disclosure of the credentials worth stealing. Compiling attacker-supplied template source is still a mistake -- this stops it being an unrecoverable one.

subsystems.name: memory
subsystems.capability: The two in-process primitives every other subsystem's memory is built on: a bounded key/value table with LRU eviction and lazy TTL, and a bounded queue in four disciplines -- FIFO, LIFO, priority, and round-robin across lanes
subsystems.policy: One bounded table and one bounded queue, so that a bound, a deadline and a claim are written once rather than per subsystem. `wreath.kv.KV` is unsynchronised on purpose -- every caller is event-loop-local and a lock would charge every reader for a race no reader has -- and `wreath.queue.Queue` is locked, because it exists for the hand-offs that do cross threads. Loss is counted, never silent: a full queue returns False and increments `dropped`, and an evicting table increments `evictions`. Expiry is lazy in both directions; nothing sweeps in the background, because a sweeper duplicates across workers and swallows its own failures. `len()` counts what the primitive will still return rather than what it happens to hold, and `count(now=...)` exists because `len()` cannot take an injected clock -- collapsing the two silently broke MemoryStore's count. The native table is a SwissTable: one control byte per slot, scanned 32 lanes at a time by the arms in `_native/simd.h`, which `simd_probe('ctrl', ...)` crosses against the scalar definition. Hot methods are METH_FASTCALL and that is load-bearing, not housekeeping -- on METH_VARARGS the wrapper's argument tuple and keyword dict cost more than the lookup they carry, and measured 0.51us against the 0.20us table underneath. Deliberately NOT migrated, each for a stated reason: `webhooks.LocalReplayStore` (evicts earliest-expiring, pinned by a randomised model test; LRU is a different contract for a replay ledger), `orm/registry._cache` (bounded by retained *bytes* as well as by count, which KV does not express), `_mcp.SessionStore` (refuses at capacity with an operator-facing message and runs a destructor per session, where KV evicts silently), and the ASGI receive queues in `server.py`/`testing.py`/`response.py` (need blocking backpressure, which a deliberately lossy queue does not have). Four queue disciplines, and they differ in who waits rather than in speed: FIFO bounds the worst case and is the default; LIFO is deliberately unfair and is a latency choice for workloads where a stale item is worthless; PriorityQueue is a bounded binary heap, stable within a priority because most items in a real workload share one, and it never compares the payload -- so an unorderable object is queueable and no `__lt__` runs under the mutex mid-sift; RoundRobin is a lane per producer with a rotating cursor, `capacity` per lane rather than total, and a required `max_lanes` because a lane name arriving from a request is otherwise an unbounded allocation a caller controls. The rotation is plain Python on purpose: it moves a cursor over a list once per item and is nowhere near the cost of the queue operation it wraps, so there is nothing there for C to do. Two bounds and an eviction record, both added for callers rather than speculatively: `max_bytes` caps the summed per-entry `cost` the caller declares, and `track_evictions` makes `take_evicted()` report what was dropped. Between them they absorbed the last two hand-written LRUs -- `orm/registry._cache` and `_pure/postgres._plans`, which were the same fifteen lines twice and differed only in what they did with the evicted entry. The driver needs the record because an evicted plan still exists on the PostgreSQL backend until a `Close ('S')` goes out for it; the registry needs nothing done with it and passes `track_evictions=False`, which costs it nothing. Only evictions are reported, never expiries or deletes: the caller already knows about those, and `clear()` reports nothing because a teardown is not an eviction -- the driver clears when the connection is going away, where the statements it would close no longer exist. `BoundedCache` and `MemoryStore` are subclasses of `KV`, not reimplementations: the first adds a `stats` property and the second the two-backend protocol's `claim`/`read` names, and everything else is inherited. That is why `KV` splits `tp_new` from `tp_init` -- a C type that configures itself in `tp_new` forces every subclass to override `__new__` and never call `super().__init__`, a rule nothing enforces. `wreath.queue.Queue` still carries that constraint and says so. Every construction of one of these under `src/wreath` must appear in `docs/reference/memory-budgets.md`; MAP013 fails the build otherwise, because a page answering 'how much does a worker hold' is worth reading only if something keeps it true. One family, one set of rules, and that is maintained deliberately: all four public types construct through `__init__` like ordinary Python classes (both C types split `tp_new` from `tp_init` for it), `clear` returns a count everywhere, `peek` means the same read-without-disturbing on all of them, and the three queues share fourteen names while differing only where they genuinely differ (`lifo`/`drop_oldest`, `drop_lowest`, `lanes`). `RoundRobin` mixes in the same `Awaiting` as the other two rather than restating the waiter and cancellation logic. The single shared name that means something different is `RoundRobin.capacity`, which is per lane; that is stated in the reference page and pinned by a test rather than smoothed over.

subsystems.name: cache
subsystems.capability: An in-process snapshot cache for read-mostly data, and HTTP response caching invalidated by the ORM writes behind it
subsystems.policy: Read-mostly application cache by atomic generation publication. Reads perform no hidden I/O; misses are explicit. Refresh is single-flight and failure preserves the previous generation. Shipped pure-first (dict-backed read path); the facade selects a native SnapshotCache only if one is measured in. `response_cache.cached` is a shared/public cache by default: it never stores a response that sets a cookie or is marked no-store/private, and a per-principal response needs an explicit `key`. Cache invalidation is driven by the ORM: a session announces the model names it wrote once its transaction commits, and caches that named those models clear. Published after commit, never before -- a rolled-back write must invalidate nothing. `cache.invalidate_across_workers(bus)` carries the same announcement to the other workers over the message bus. Subscribers (react to a write) and bridges (carry it off-worker) are separate lists so a received announcement is applied locally and never relayed onward; a bridge failure cannot fail a committed write, and cross-worker delivery is at-most-once, leaving the TTL as the backstop. `cache.refresh_on(snapshot, [Model], load=...)` puts the SnapshotCache on the same event: reference data *reloads* rather than dropping (a dropped generation is an explicit miss on data that still exists), single-flight, and a failing loader leaves the previous generation in place. Both halves go fleet-wide through the one `invalidate_across_workers` bridge. `BoundedCache` is now a shell over `wreath.kv.KV` (the `memory` subsystem) rather than its own OrderedDict; the note in `cache.py` that used to refuse a native twin records why that changed and what it had measured.

subsystems.name: doctor
subsystems.capability: Runtime diagnostics for your own handlers, including the N+1 query you did not know you had
subsystems.policy: Defects a green test suite cannot see, over layers only Wreath holds together. Scopes: a request is not the only one, and is not the worst. `_nplusone.watching(origin, limit)` binds a ledger for any execution scope; `_nplusone.scope_for(origin, budget=...)` holds the three-state rule in one place -- a declared `query_budget` fails at the ceiling, no budget but a guard already in the process observes and reports, neither binds nothing at all. `wreath.jobs` binds one per job *attempt* (a retry starts from zero, or a task that legitimately queries ninety times dead-letters itself on the second try), `wreath.workflows` one per step plus a separate one per compensation, `wreath.passes` one per shift rather than per chunk -- an N+1 inside a hundred-row chunk is under any per-chunk ceiling a person would write, and it is the product of queries-per-chunk and chunks-per-shift that turns a backfill into an outage. Failing is opt-in everywhere outside a request: a guard that raises inside a durable job turns a slow job into a failed one and then into a retry storm. `NPlusOneGuard` deliberately does *not* use `watching` -- the middleware protocol splits bind and reset across two calls, and a suspended `@contextmanager` held on `request.state` is finalized when the request object becomes unreachable, which unbinds the ledger mid-request rather than at the end of it. N+1: the ORM stamps each read's model onto the recorder's ORM_HYDRATE phase (dependency_id = the metadata image's model entry id, stamped onto `Registry._flight_model_ids` at startup like a Database's `_flight_dep_id`), and the completion carries the route, so a trace can name the shape rather than only the endpoint. Two surfaces, one vocabulary: `NPlusOneGuard` trips inside the query that crossed the limit so the traceback names the loop, and `diagnose_n_plus_one` / `wreath doctor n-plus-one` reads the same finding out of a running server's Inspector without reproducing anything. Both produce a `Finding`. Cost discipline: the ORM seam reads no ContextVar until a guard exists (`_nplusone.WATCHING`, a module attribute, not a crossing) and reads no phase marker until a metadata image exists (`_flight_model_ids` non-empty), so `wreath-request-trace` records zero added crossings for an app that uses neither. The guard is for development and staging; a guard that fails production requests is a worse outage than the N+1.

subsystems.name: temporal
subsystems.capability: Timezone-correct dates, times, and durations across the request boundary and the database
subsystems.policy: An `Instant` is always aware; a naive value is refused, never assumed UTC -- that assumption is the bug the module exists to prevent. Dependency-free over stdlib datetime/zoneinfo, because the core cannot take arrow and those are the applications being ported. One declaration settles every surface: ORM column, binding coercion, REST JSON, OpenAPI format, typegen alias, GraphQL scalar -- they used to be five places that drifted. Temporal JSON encoding is a *retry* in the `_json` facade (encode as-is; only a TypeError triggers rewrite-and-retry), never a pre-pass, so a payload with no timestamps pays one un-raised try and the ordinary response path is untouched. Body validation is deliberately NOT wired: it has a byte-for-byte C twin in `_native/validate.c`, and a silent divergence there is worse than the gap. The relative formatter is the single locale-keyed seam, so i18n is a table entry rather than a migration. ISO durations reject years/months: neither is a fixed number of seconds and a timedelta cannot hold one honestly.

subsystems.name: geospatial
subsystems.capability: Coordinates, great-circle distances, and index-answerable proximity bounds, with no PostgreSQL extension
subsystems.policy: A `Coordinate` is keyword-only and a bare pair is refused, for the reason `wreath.temporal` refuses a naive datetime: GeoJSON orders [lon, lat], humans say 'lat, lon', and a positional pair silently picks one -- the symptom is not an exception, it is a wrong place. Bounds are inclusive, since the poles and the antimeridian are real coordinates.
